summary: Describes specifics for applying Signaling Compression to SIP, such as default minimum parameter values, state management, and issues over TCP. Implementations must also support the SIP and SDP static dictionary. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary:
SigComp compresses a message by sending a short program to the other end, which runs it to rebuild the original. The framework says nothing about which application is being compressed, so each application needs its own set of rules.

This RFC supplies those rules for SIP. It sets how much memory a SIP endpoint must set aside, says that compressed and uncompressed SIP can share a port, names each endpoint so the two sides know they are talking to the same peer, and ties the memory holding compression state to the lifetime of a SIP registration.

questions: how big must sigcomp decompression memory be for sip
when does a sip sigcomp compartment close
subtitle: How the SigComp compression layer is applied to SIP, with the settings, compartments and rules SIP needs.

tldr.problem: SigComp is a generic compression framework, but it deliberately leaves out everything specific to the application using it. Without that detail, two SIP endpoints could compress the same way and still fail to understand each other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC binds SigComp to SIP. It raises the minimum decompressor and state memory, requires the SIP and SDP static dictionary and the NACK mechanism, defines how each end names itself with a sigcomp-id parameter, and ties the lifetime of a compression compartment to SIP registration state.
tldr.outcome: SIP compression has one agreed set of parameters and rules rather than a dozen local interpretations. RFC 3486 was updated, and RFC 8996 later updated this document.

today: RFC 5049 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted. It updated RFC 3486, and it was later updated by RFC 8996, which deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1.

sections.title: What SIP/SigComp Adds
sections.content:
SigComp is a solution for compressing messages generated by application protocols. Although its primary driver is to compress SIP messages, the solution itself has been intentionally designed to be application agnostic so that it can be applied to any application protocol, which is denoted as ANY/SigComp. Consequently, many application-dependent specifics are left out of the base standard. It is intended that a separate specification be used to describe those specifics when SigComp is applied to a particular application protocol.

This document binds SigComp and SIP, which is denoted as SIP/SigComp. Any SigComp implementation used for the compression of SIP messages MUST conform to this document as well as to the base SigComp specification. It must also support the SIP and SDP static dictionary and the mechanism for discovering SigComp support at the SIP layer.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: SigComp works for any application, so it says nothing about SIP specifics. This document fills that gap, and it also sets the floor for the memory an endpoint must have.

sections.title: Minimum Parameter Values for SIP
sections.content:
SigComp defines a few parameters that describe SigComp behaviour, and the base specification gives each one a minimum value that any endpoint MUST support. Those minimum values were chosen with all imaginable devices in mind, and scalability was considered a key factor. Some of them are too small to allow good performance for SIP message compression, so they are increased for SIP/SigComp. The new minimum values are specific to SIP/SigComp and do not apply to any other application protocols. An endpoint MAY offer additional resources over and above the minimum values if available.

decompression_memory_size (DMS) has a minimum of 2048 bytes for ANY/SigComp and 8192 bytes for SIP/SigComp. The reason given is that 2048 bytes is too small for SIP message compression, as it seriously limits the compression ratio and even makes compression impossible for certain messages. The condition set for SigComp over UDP is C + 2*B + R + 2*S + 128 < DMS, where C is the size of the compressed application message depending on R, B is the size of the bytecode, R is the size of the circular buffer in UDVM memory, S is any additional state uploaded other than that created from the content of the circular buffer at the end of decompression, and 128 is the smallest address in UDVM memory to copy bytecode to. If DMS is too small, at least one of C, B, R or S will be severely restricted. DMS is memory that is only temporarily needed during decompression, so a requirement of 8 KB should not cause problems for an endpoint that already implements SIP and SigComp.

state_memory_size (SMS) has a minimum of zero bytes for ANY/SigComp and 2048 bytes for SIP/SigComp. A non-zero SMS allows an endpoint to upload a state in the first SIP message sent to a remote endpoint without the uncertainty of whether the remote endpoint will have enough memory to store such a state. Based on the observation that there is little gain from stateless SigComp compression, the assumption is that purely stateless SIP implementations are unlikely to provide a SigComp function. SMS applies to each individual compartment, and an endpoint MAY offer different values for different compartments as long as the value is not less than 2048 bytes.

cycles_per_bit (CPB) has a minimum of 16 for both ANY/SigComp and SIP/SigComp. SigComp_version (SV) is 0x01 for ANY/SigComp and at least 0x02 for SIP/SigComp, meaning SigComp plus NACK. That implies that decompression failures result in SigComp NACK messages sent back to the originating compressor, and that the compressor need not make use of the methods for detecting support for NACK, for example it can use optimistic compression methods right from the outset. locally available state (LAS) is none for ANY/SigComp and the SIP/SDP static dictionary for SIP/SigComp. Since support for the static SIP/SDP dictionary is mandatory, it does not need to be advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: Four settings are raised above the generic minimums. A SIP endpoint needs eight kilobytes of scratch memory to decompress into, rather than two, and two kilobytes of state per compartment rather than none, so that it can remember things between messages and get a better compression ratio. The dictionary of common SIP words is mandatory, and so is the NACK mechanism that reports a decompression failure back to the sender.

sections.title: Sharing a Port Between Compressed and Uncompressed SIP
sections.content:
To limit the number of ports required by a SigComp-aware endpoint, both SigComp messages and vanilla SIP messages, that is uncompressed SIP messages with no SigComp header, may arrive on the same port.

For a message-based transport such as UDP or SCTP, distinguishing between SigComp and non-SigComp messages can be done per message. The receiving endpoint checks the first octet of the UDP or SCTP payload to determine whether the message has been compressed using SigComp. If the Most Significant Bits of the octet are 11111, the message is considered to be a SigComp message and is parsed as such. If the MSBs take any other value, the message is assumed to be an uncompressed SIP message and is passed directly to the application with no further effect on the SigComp layer.

For a stream-based transport such as TCP, the distinction has to be made per connection. The receiving endpoint checks the first octet of the TCP data stream: if the MSBs are 11111 the stream is considered to contain SigComp messages, and otherwise it is assumed to contain uncompressed SIP messages. SigComp message delimiters MUST NOT be used if the stream contains uncompressed SIP messages.

Applications MUST NOT mix SIP messages and SigComp messages on a single TCP connection. If the TCP connection is used to carry SigComp messages, then all messages sent over the connection MUST have a SigComp header and be delimited by the use of 0xFFFF. A set of bytecodes in the SigComp corrections and clarifications document implements a null decompression algorithm, which effectively allows SigComp peers to send selected SigComp messages with uncompressed data. If a SIP implementation has reason to send both compressed and uncompressed SIP messages on a single TCP connection, the compressor can be instructed to use these bytecodes so that the uncompressed messages are also valid SigComp messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The first byte of a datagram decides: if its top five bits are all ones, the message is compressed, and otherwise it is ordinary SIP. Over TCP the same test is applied once to the whole connection, so a connection carries one kind or the other and never both.

sections.title: Messages That Do Not Fit, and Retransmissions
sections.content:
SigComp does not support the compression of messages larger than 64k. If a SIP application sending compressed SIP messages over a transport connection needs to send a SIP message larger than 64k, the application MUST NOT send it over the same TCP connection. The application SHOULD send it over a different transport connection, which may mean establishing a new one.

When SIP messages are retransmitted, they need to be re-compressed, taking into account any SigComp states that may have been created or invalidated since the previous transmission. Implementations MUST NOT cache the result of compressing the message and retransmit such a cached result. The reason is that it is impossible to know whether the failure causing the retransmission occurred on the message being retransmitted or on the response to that message. If the response was lost, any state changes effected by the first instance of the retransmitted message would already have taken place, and if those changes removed a state that the previously transmitted message relied upon, retransmission of the same compressed message would lead to a decompression failure.

A SIP retransmission may be caused by the original message or its response being lost through a decompression failure. In that case a NACK will have been sent by the decompressor to the compressor, which may use the information in the NACK to adjust its compression parameters. On an unreliable transport such a NACK may still be lost, so a compressor that used optimistic compression MAY want to switch to a method less likely to cause a decompression failure when compressing a SIP retransmission.

Section 6 of the document also rules out Continuous Mode over TCP. Continuous mode is a special feature of SigComp designed to improve the overall compression ratio for long-lived connections, and its use requires pre-agreement between the compressor and the decompressor. It is not used with SIP/SigComp because it requires the transport itself to provide a certain level of protection against denial-of-service attacks, and TCP alone is not considered to provide enough protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A message bigger than 64 kilobytes cannot be compressed, so it has to travel on another connection. A retransmitted message must be compressed again rather than resent from a cache, because the first attempt may already have changed the state that the cached copy relied on.

sections.title: Identifying Remote Applications
sections.content:
An application exchanging compressed traffic with a remote application has a compartment that contains the state information needed to compress outgoing messages and decompress incoming messages. To increase compression efficiency, the application must assign distinct compartments to distinct remote applications.

SIP/SigComp applications identify remote applications by their SIP/SigComp identifiers. Each SIP/SigComp application MUST have a SIP/SigComp identifier URN that uniquely identifies the application, and this URN MUST be persistent as long as the application stores compartment state related to other SIP/SigComp applications. An application SHOULD use a UUID URN as its identifier, due to the difficulties in equality comparisons for other kinds of URNs. If a URN scheme other than UUID is used, the URN MUST be selected such that the application can be certain that no other SIP/SigComp application would choose the same value. A device with a globally unique instance identifier SHOULD use that identifier as its SIP/SigComp identifier, because it improves the compression ratio of header fields that carry both identifiers. Server farms that share SIP/SigComp state across servers MUST use the same identifier for all their servers.

The identifiers are carried in the sigcomp-id SIP URI or Via header field parameter. The SIP URI parameter is a uri-parameter as defined by the SIP ABNF, with the syntax uri-sip-sigcomp-id = "sigcomp-id=" 1*paramchar. The Via parameter is a via-extension, with the syntax via-sip-sigcomp-id = "sigcomp-id" EQUAL LDQUOT *( qdtext / quoted-pair ) RDQUOT. Both MUST contain a URN. An example of the URI parameter is sigcomp-id=urn:uuid:0C67446E-F1A1-11D9-94D3-000A95A0E128.

SIP messages are matched with remote application identifiers as follows. For an outgoing request, the remote application identifier is the SIP/SigComp identifier of the URI to which the request is sent; if the URI has no identifier, it is the IP address plus port of the datagram for connectionless transports, or the transport connection for connection-oriented ones. For an incoming response it is the same as that of the request that started the transaction. For an incoming request it is the identifier in the top-most Via entry, falling back in the same way to the source address or the transport connection. For an outgoing response it is the same as that of the request that started the transaction. An application placing its URI with the comp=sigcomp parameter in a header field MUST add a sigcomp-id parameter with its identifier to that URI, and an application generating its own Via entry containing comp=sigcomp MUST add a sigcomp-id parameter to that Via entry.

Equality comparisons between identifiers are performed using the URN equality rules for the scheme. If the element performing the comparisons does not understand the URN scheme, it uses the lexical equality rules of RFC 2141, which may result in two URNs being considered unequal when they are actually equal. Because the only element that provides the URN is the application identified by it, the application SHOULD provide lexically equivalent URNs in each registration it generates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint gives itself a unique name, normally a UUID written as a URN, and puts it in the requests it sends. The two ends then know which compartment, and which saved state, to use for each other. The name has to stay the same for as long as any state is kept.

sections.title: Opening and Closing Compartments
sections.content:
The lifetime of SIP/SigComp compartments is linked to registration state. Compartments are opened at SIP registration time and are typically closed when the registration expires or is cancelled. Linking the lifetime of compartments to registration state limits the applicability of the specification: SIP user agents that do not register, for example those that only handle PUBLISH or SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY transactions, cannot create compartments following this specification. Previous revisions also defined compartments valid during a SIP transaction or a SIP dialog, which covered all possible SIP entities, but those types were eliminated because the complexity they introduced, such as edge proxy servers being required to keep dialog state, was higher than the benefits they brought in most deployment scenarios.

Usually, any states created during the lifetime of a compartment are logically deleted when the compartment is closed. A logical deletion can become a physical deletion only when no compartment continues to exist that created the same state. A SigComp endpoint may offer to keep a state created on request from a peer beyond the default lifetime of a compartment, and can signal this by announcing the partial state ID in the returned SigComp parameters at the end of the registration that was supposed to limit the lifetime of the state. The mandatory support for the NACK mechanism ensures that it is possible to recover from synchronisation errors regarding compartment lifetimes.

As an operational concern, bugs in the compartment management implementation are likely to lead to sporadic, hard-to-diagnose failures. Decompressors may therefore want to cache old state and, if still available, allow access while logging diagnostic information, and both compressors and decompressors use the NACK mechanism to recover when such old state is no longer available.

A REGISTER transaction causes an application to open a new compartment valid for the duration of the registration. An application that needs to send a compressed SIP REGISTER SHOULD open a compartment for the request's remote application identifier, and an application that receives a compressed SIP REGISTER SHOULD open a compartment for the request's remote application identifier. These compartments MAY be closed if the REGISTER request is responded to with a non-2xx final response, or when the registration expires or is cancelled. Applications MAY also choose to keep them open for longer. For a given successful registration, applications SHOULD NOT close their associated compartments until the registration is over.

If an application is supposed to open a compartment for a remote application identifier for which it already has one, for example when it registers towards a second registrar using the same edge proxy server, the application MUST use the already existing compartment and MUST NOT open a new one.

If a SIP application does not have a compartment for a message it needs to send, it MAY choose not to compress it even in the presence of the comp=sigcomp parameter. Stateless compression is not typically worthwhile and may even result in message expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: A compartment is the memory that holds what the two ends have learned about each other. It is created when the endpoint registers and is normally thrown away when the registration ends. The rules exist so that both ends agree on when that happens, because a mismatch would show up as an occasional decompression failure that is hard to trace.

sections.title: Recommendations for Network Administrators
sections.content:
Network administrators can configure their networks so that the compression efficiency achieved is increased. For a given user agent, the route sets for incoming requests, created by a Path header field, and for outgoing requests, created by a Service-Route header field, are typically the same. Registrars can, if they wish, insert proxies in one route that do not appear in the other and vice versa. It is RECOMMENDED that registrars are configured so that proxies performing SigComp compression appear in both routes.

The routes described apply to requests sent outside a dialog. Requests inside a dialog follow a route constructed using Record-Route header fields. It is RECOMMENDED that the proxies performing SigComp that are in the route for requests outside a dialog are configured to place themselves, by inserting themselves in the Record-Route header fields, in the routes used for requests inside dialogs.

When a user agent's registration expires, proxy servers performing compression may close their associated compartment. If the user agent is involved in a dialog that was established before the registration expired, subsequent requests within the dialog may not be compressed any longer. To avoid this, it is RECOMMENDED that user agents are registered as long as they are involved in a dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression only pays off if the same proxy handles both directions of the traffic. The RFC therefore asks that the compressing proxy be on the path for requests arriving and leaving, and that endpoints keep registering while a call is up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The same security considerations as described in the base SigComp specification apply to this document. Keeping SigComp states longer than the duration of a SIP dialog should not pose new security risks, because the state has been allowed to be created in the first place.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual SigComp security rules apply, and keeping compression state a little longer than the call is not a new risk, since the state was allowed in the first place.

items.title: Look at the first byte
items.text: If its five most significant bits are 11111 the message is a SigComp message; otherwise it is ordinary SIP.

items.title: Per message on UDP
items.text: On UDP and SCTP each datagram is classified on its own.

items.title: Per connection on TCP
items.text: On TCP the first octet of the stream decides for the whole connection.

items.title: Never mix on one TCP connection
items.text: A TCP connection carries either SigComp messages or plain SIP messages, never both.
